message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a residential tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Category | What the law says | Practical Tips | |----------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlords may charge a security deposit, but it cannot exceed **one month’s rent** for a month‑to‑month lease or **two months’ rent** for a lease of longer duration.
• The deposit must be held in a **separate, interest‑bearing account** (unless the landlord is a Texas bank).
• Within **30 days** after you move out, the landlord must return the deposit (or provide a written itemized list of deductions) and pay any interest earned. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any deposit receipts.
• Take photos or videos of the unit before you move out. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition**. This includes functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural integrity.
• The landlord must repair any major defects within a reasonable time after notice. | • Report problems in writing (email or text) and keep a copy.
• If the landlord fails to act, you may file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or pursue a “repair‑and‑deduct” remedy (see below). | | **Repair‑and‑Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to repair a major defect, you may **pay for the repair yourself** and deduct the cost from your rent, provided the repair is necessary for habitability and you give the landlord written notice. | • Keep receipts and document the issue.
• The deduction cannot exceed the actual cost of the repair. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to live in the unit without unreasonable interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • If the landlord enters the unit without proper notice (usually 24 hrs for non‑emergencies), you can refuse entry. | | **Notice Requirements** | • **Month‑to‑month**: 30‑day written notice to terminate.
• **Fixed‑term lease**: The lease specifies the termination date; otherwise, a 30‑day notice is required if the lease ends. | • Provide notice in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Rent Increases** | • For month‑to‑month leases, the landlord may raise rent at the start of a new lease term, but must give **30‑day written notice**.
• For fixed‑term leases, rent is fixed unless the lease allows increases. | • Review the lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Discrimination** | • Under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas law, landlords cannot discriminate based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, or source of income (e.g., public assistance). | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlords must follow the **Texas Property Code**: provide a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you do not comply, the landlord can file an eviction lawsuit (unlawful detainer). | • Respond promptly to notices.
• If you believe the eviction is unlawful, seek legal aid or a tenant‑rights group. | | **Privacy** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hrs) before entering the unit, except in emergencies. | • Keep a log of any entries. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. If the landlord pays, they must maintain the utility service. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Lease Modifications** | • Any changes to the lease must be in writing and signed by both parties. | • Do not sign a modified lease until you read and agree to all changes. | | **Legal Assistance** | • Texas has several nonprofit tenant‑rights organizations (e.g., Texas Tenants Union, Texas Legal Services Center). | • Contact them for free or low‑cost legal help. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the entire lease** – look for clauses on rent, deposits, repairs, and termination. 2. **Confirm the security deposit limit** – it should not exceed one month’s rent (or two for longer leases). 3. **Ask about utilities** – who pays what? 4. **Check for “no‑entry” clauses** – how much notice is required? 5. **Verify the landlord’s contact info** – ensure you can reach them easily. 6. **Document the unit’s condition** – take photos or a video walkthrough. ### When Things Go Wrong | Issue | First Step | Next Step | |-------|------------|-----------| | Landlord fails to repair a major defect | Write a notice (email/text) and keep a copy | If no action, consider repair‑and‑deduct or file a complaint with TDHCA | | Unreasonable entry | Ask the landlord to provide notice | If repeated, consult a lawyer or tenant‑rights group | | Discrimination | File a complaint with HUD or Texas Commission on Human Rights | Seek legal representation if needed | | Unlawful eviction notice | Respond in writing, ask for clarification | File a lawsuit in the county court if the eviction proceeds | --- **Remember:** While this table covers many common rights, individual circumstances can vary. If you’re facing a specific problem—like a disputed deposit, a potential eviction, or a serious habitability issue—consider reaching out to a local tenant‑rights organization or a qualified attorney for tailored guidance.
